Step 3: Finding the P-value of the Test

children.label: Step 3: Finding the P-value of the Test

children.value: So far we’ve talked about the p-value at the intuitive level: understanding what it is (or what it measures) and how we use it to draw conclusions about the significance of our results. We will now go more deeply into how the p-value is calculated.

It should be mentioned that eventually we will rely on technology to calculate the p-value for us (as well as the test statistic), but in order to make intelligent use of the output, it is important to first
the details, and only then let the computer do the calculations for us. Let’s start.

children.value: One can actually draw conclusions in hypothesis testing just using the test statistic, and as we’ll see, the p-value is, in a sense, just another way of looking at the test statistic. The reason that we take the extra step in this course and derive the p-value from the test statistic is that even though in this case (the test about the population proportion) and some other tests, the value of the test statistic has a very clear and intuitive interpretation, there are some tests where its value is not as easy to interpret. On the other hand, the p-value keeps its intuitive appeal across all statistical tests.

(Examples: if z = −2.5, the p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as small as −2.5 or smaller, or as large as 2.5 or larger. If z = 1.5, the p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as large as 1.5 or larger, or as small as −1.5 or smaller.)

As noted earlier, before the widespread use of statistical software, it was common to use

instead of p-values to assess the evidence provided by the data. In that approach, the observed test statistic is compared with a fixed cutoff value (for example, z* = 1.645 for a one-sided test at the 0.05 level), and

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: is rejected when the test statistic falls beyond the cutoff. The two approaches always lead to the same conclusion; this course focuses on p-values.
On the next page, we will apply the p-value to our three examples. But first, work through the following activities, which should help your understanding.
Check Your Understanding: Finding the P-value

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Finding the P-value

model.question: A test of H₀: p = 0.30 versus Hₐ: p > 0.30 yields a test statistic of z = 1.8. Which area under the standard normal curve equals the p-value?

choices.text: The area to the right of 1.8
choices.feedback: Correct! For Hₐ: p > p₀, the p-value is the area to the RIGHT of the observed z: P(Z ≥ 1.8).

choices.text: The area to the left of 1.8
choices.feedback: The area to the left would be appropriate for a "less than" alternative.

choices.text: The area beyond ±1.8 in both tails
choices.feedback: Two tails are only used for a "not equal to" alternative.

model.question: A test of H₀: p = 0.30 versus Hₐ: p ≠ 0.30 yields a test statistic of z = −2.1. Which area equals the p-value?

choices.text: The area to the left of −2.1 plus the area to the right of 2.1
choices.feedback: Correct! For a two-sided alternative, the p-value is the area in BOTH tails: P(Z ≤ −2.1) + P(Z ≥ 2.1) = 2P(Z ≥ 2.1).

choices.text: The area to the left of −2.1 only
choices.feedback: The left tail alone would be the p-value for Hₐ: p < 0.30.
The area between −2.1 and 2.1 is everything EXCEPT the p-value.

model.question: Two tests each produce a test statistic of z = 2.0—one tests Hₐ: p > p₀ and the other tests Hₐ: p ≠ p₀. How do their p-values compare?

choices.text: The two-sided test has a p-value twice as large as the one-sided test
choices.feedback: Correct! The one-tailed p-value is P(Z ≥ 2) ≈ 0.023, while the two-tailed p-value doubles it: ≈ 0.046.

choices.text: The one-sided test has a p-value twice as large as the two-sided test
choices.feedback: The two-sided test's p-value is twice as large, since it includes both tails.
The p-values differ because the definition of "extreme" differs between the two alternatives.

model.hint: The two-tailed p-value counts the area in both tails.

model.question: Why is a SMALLER p-value stronger evidence against H₀?

choices.text: Because it means data like ours would be very unlikely if H₀ were true
choices.feedback: Correct! A tiny p-value says data like ours would almost never occur if H₀ were true—so the fact that we observed such data discredits H₀.

choices.text: Because it is the probability that H₀ is true
choices.feedback: The p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true; it is a probability about the DATA, computed assuming H₀ is true.

choices.text: Because it means the data agree closely with H₀
choices.feedback: A small p-value indicates the data are FAR from what H₀ predicts, not close to it.

model.hint: The p-value measures how likely data like ours would be in a world where H₀ is true.

children.value: Check Your Understanding: P-values and Tails

children.label: Check Your Understanding: P-values and Tails

model.question: A figure shows a standard normal curve with only the area to the LEFT of z = −1.4 shaded. Which pair of hypotheses and test statistic matches the figure?

choices.feedback: Correct! A left-tailed shaded region corresponds to Hₐ: p < p₀ with an observed z = −1.4.
A "greater than" alternative would shade to the right.
A two-sided alternative would shade both tails.

model.hint: A single shaded left tail corresponds to a "less than" alternative.
